summary: This informational document formally records an existing public key file format used to exchange public keys between different SSH implementations. It also defines a standard text form for SSH public key fingerprints. It was later updated by RFC 9519.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4716 describes a text format for moving SSH public keys between programs. It also records a short fingerprint format that people can use when checking a public key.

what headers can an ssh public key file have
subtitle: A text-file format for exchanging SSH public keys and displaying their fingerprints.

tldr.problem: SSH public-key authentication requires clients and servers to exchange public keys, but implementations needed a common file format.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a text file with begin and end markers, optional headers, and a base64-encoded key body. It also describes a colon-separated MD5 fingerprint representation.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents an existing format and is Informational, not a standard. It has been updated by RFC 9519.

today: RFC 4716 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 9519.

sections.title: Why Public Keys Need a File Format
sections.content:
SSH can authenticate with public and private key pairs, but the public keys must first be exchanged between client and server. RFC 4716 describes an existing text-file format that can be transferred using common file-transfer mechanisms.

The RFC also describes a short text representation of a public key called a fingerprint. It is intended to make checking a long public host key easier for a person.
sections.plainLanguage: Before SSH public-key authentication can work, the two sides need to exchange public keys. This RFC describes a shared file layout and a short way to display a key's fingerprint.

sections.title: The Public-Key File Layout
sections.content:
A key file is a sequence of text lines, each no longer than 72 8-bit bytes excluding the line ending. The first line must be ---- BEGIN SSH2 PUBLIC KEY ----, and the last must be ---- END SSH2 PUBLIC KEY ----.

Between these markers, a file may contain header fields followed by the base64-encoded public-key data specified by RFC 4253. Readers should accept common line endings: CR, LF, or CRLF. The file body also follows the 72-byte line limit.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key goes between two required marker lines. The key data is written as base64 text, with short lines so different systems can read the file.

sections.title: Headers and Optional Comments
sections.content:
Header fields use the form Header-tag: Header-value. Tags are case-insensitive and use US-ASCII; values use UTF-8. A line ending in a backslash continues onto the next line. The RFC defines Subject for the login name associated with the key and Comment for a user-provided note.

Tags beginning with x- are reserved for private use. Implementations must ignore unknown tags and should preserve them when editing a file. The RFC notes that this format resembles PEM and OpenPGP armor but differs in its markers, spacing, checksum, and continuation rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Optional labels can identify the key's subject or provide a comment. Programs should preserve labels they do not recognize so editing a file does not erase information.

sections.title: Displaying a Public-Key Fingerprint
sections.content:
The fingerprint is calculated by applying the MD5 message-digest algorithm to the public-key data defined by RFC 4253. The result is displayed as 16 octets in lowercase hexadecimal, separated by colons.

The fingerprint is a short representation of the key data, not the key itself. The RFC says this method was already in common use in the SSH community and formally describes its textual representation.
sections.plainLanguage: A fingerprint is a short text value calculated from the public key. It gives people a more manageable string to compare than the full key file.

sections.title: Protect Files and Review Comments
sections.content:
The file format has no built-in way to detect changes or tampering. The RFC recommends protecting key files with system access controls and transferring them over a trusted channel.

Header fields may disclose information about a user, key, or its use, so sites should review the information placed there. The fingerprint method uses MD5; the RFC notes known collision-resistance weaknesses and states that this use depends on second-preimage resistance and historical practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The format does not protect a file from being changed, so access to the file and its transfer should be protected. Comments can also reveal information, and fingerprints use the hash method described by the RFC.
